lec05kp12-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp12-u01-p8-title.text: The exact shared-window formula, boundaries and the shared gradient

lec05kp12-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp12-u01-p8-bridge.text: 36 positions: 360 parameters without sharing, 10 with it. What is the exact formula of the shared window, and how are boundaries and the gradient handled?

lec05kp12-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp12-u01-p8-c1.text: **Exact formula**: image $x$, kernel $K$, bias $b$ (cross-correlation, kernel not flipped): $r_{ij}=b+\sum_{a=0}^{2}\sum_{c=0}^{2}K_{ac}\,x_{i+a,\,j+c}$. $i,j$ is the window's top-left corner, $a,c$ the row and column offsets in the kernel; with an activation $\phi$, $F(x)_{ij}=\phi(r_{ij})$.

lec05kp12-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp12-u01-p8-c2.text: **Boundaries**: the equivariance formula needs all corresponding positions to be valid. When an object leaves the picture, padding differs, or the shift does not match the stride, equality may hold only in the interior; a rotation may also need interpolation.

lec05kp12-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp12-u01-p8-c3.text: **Shared gradient**: a parameter $k$ enters many scores $r_p$ and the chain rule adds the paths: $\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial k}=\sum_p\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial r_p}\dfrac{\partial r_p}{\partial k}$; for a locally linear score $\partial r_p/\partial k=x_p$.

steps.label: Weight sharing and transformation invariance
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp12 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first (which figure covers which lecture sections) and each page is mainly one native infographic; the symbols and terms are defined inside the same figure. This unit is self-study: 5 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Every number is computed by code. English version.

steps.label: The weight-sharing idea
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of weight sharing in chapter 4. The idea: a stroke moved elsewhere is still the same class, but we do not require every number in the network to stay fixed. Two steps: first limit every unit to a small area, the receptive field; then let all positions use one set of weights, weight sharing, and this weight matrix is the kernel, written K. First row of the figure: the 6 by 6 image x has a three-cell vertical stroke in column 1; the yellow frame is one 3 by 3 window; the middle column of K is 1 and the rest 0; the score of the window is 1 times 1 plus 1 times 1 plus 1 times 1, which is 3. Second row: shifting the image right by two columns gives Tx with the stroke in column 3; what we want is an unchanged class, c of Tx equals c of x, which is transformation invariance. The next page asks what we get when the kernel slides over the whole image, and how that changes after the shift.

steps.label: Equivariance and invariance
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed one set of weights sliding over the image with a window score of 3. This page asks how the whole feature map changes. Apply the kernel K to every window and arrange the sixteen scores as a 4 by 4 feature map: for x the bright column is column 0 with scores 2, 3, 2, 1 from top to bottom; for the shifted Tx the bright column is column 2 with the same numbers. The response moves with the stroke, which is translation equivariance, written F of Tx equals T applied to F of x. Taking only the maximum of the whole map is global max pooling; both maps give 3, so the readout no longer depends on position, and that is invariance. Limits: the shift must be complete and the boundary and stride compatible; pooling throws position away. The next page asks how many parameters sharing saves and how the shared weight is updated in training.

steps.label: Parameters and the update
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the feature map moving with the stroke and the maximum giving an invariant readout. This page asks how many parameters are saved when sixteen positions share one set of weights. On the left, not shared: each of 16 positions has 9 weights and 1 bias, 16 times 10 is 160; on the right, shared: all positions use 9 plus 1, which is 10. The computing is still 16 times; what is saved is adjustable numbers, not work. The three boxes below show how a shared weight is updated: the shared weight k enters the scores of many positions and the chain rule adds up the paths, so the total gradient is the sum of delta p times x p over positions; two positions give 0.2 times 3 and minus 0.1 times 1, a total of 0.5; with learning rate 0.1 and old k equal to 1 the update is 1 minus 0.1 times 0.5, which is 0.95, and every position then uses 0.95. The next page asks which routes besides sharing make a classifier insensitive to a transformation.

steps.label: Three routes to invariance
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed sharing cutting the adjustable parameters to 10 while the computing stays 16. This page asks which routes besides sharing make a classifier insensitive to a transformation. There are three and they can be combined, but first decide whether the transformation keeps the class. First, invariant features: turn the data into a representation insensitive to the given transformation; the risk is losing information needed to recognise. Second, architecture constraints: share weights and pool suitably, explicitly forcing certain computations to be equal; the risk is that it only holds for compatible transformations. Third, data augmentation: generate more training examples with sensible transformations; the risk is that finite examples rarely guarantee invariance under every transformation. The next page asks what shifts and rotations each keep when pixels are multiplied in pairs.

steps.label: When shift and rotation can be shared
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the three routes, each starting with whether the transformation keeps the class. This page asks what shifts and rotations each keep when pixels are multiplied in pairs. The score of a higher-order network contains products of inputs, and the coefficient of a pixel pair can be shared by geometry. Left: under a shift both ends move by t so the difference vector is unchanged, hence pairs with the same displacement can share a coefficient; the two blue lines both have displacement (1,1) and can share, while the orange line has displacement (2,2) and, although the slope is the same, cannot. Middle: a rotation keeps length, so pairs of equal length can share a second-order coefficient; (1,0) and (0,1) lie on the same circle. Right: the squared norm is rotation-invariant, both points give 1; but adding the linear term a equal to (1,0) the two scores are b plus 1 plus c and b plus c, which differ, so one symmetric term does not make the whole model symmetric. The next page is an extension: counting practice on an 8 by 8 image.

steps.label: Extension: exercise
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page covered when shifts and rotations can be shared. This page is the exercise: question 1, an 8 by 8 input, 3 by 3 window, stride 1, no padding, the bias shared too: how large is the feature map and how many parameters with and without sharing? Question 2: after sharing, the high-scoring position moves with the input; is that equivariance or invariance? Pause and work it out; the next page is the solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two questions. Question 1: 8 minus 3 plus 1 is 6 positions per direction, 36 in all, a 6 by 6 feature map; without sharing it is 36 times 10, which is 360; with sharing it is 9 plus 1, which is 10; a bigger image only adds uses, not shared parameters. Question 2: a high score that follows the input is equivariance; only with suitable pooling and the right conditions can it become invariance. The next page is an extension: the exact formula of the shared window, boundaries and the gradient.

steps.label: Extension: exact formula and boundaries
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page worked out 36 positions, 360 parameters without sharing and 10 with it. This page asks what the exact formula of the shared window is and how boundaries and the gradient are handled. The exact formula: the score r ij is the bias b plus the sum of kernel entries times the corresponding window entries, with i and j the top-left corner of the window. Boundaries: equivariance needs every corresponding position to be valid; when an object leaves the picture or padding differs, equality may hold only in the interior. Shared gradient: one parameter enters many scores and the chain rule adds the paths. This is the last page of the unit; the next unit is KP13.
